title_en: On the Soul, Against the Philosophers
author: Eustathius of Antioch
occasion: Eustathius argues against philosophical teachings, especially those associated with Pythagoreans and Platonists, that the soul is unbegotten and pre-exists the body, and that souls drink from the water of forgetfulness before birth. He writes to refute these views and to show from observable human development and from Scripture that the soul is created and grows with the body.
argument: Eustathius first establishes that God fills all things and is not confined by place, and that the divine is not subject to fixed laws and times; this appears to be directed against philosophical conceptions that would limit God, setting up the contrast with the philosophers' own self-contradictory myths. He then attacks the myth of the water of forgetfulness with a dilemma: if the philosophers escaped the drink of deception, then many others obviously did too, so the myth fails to explain universal ignorance; if they drank the water of forgetfulness along with everyone else, how and from what source do they fabricate myths about souls? Either way they are ignorant: if they did not experience the waters, they do not know of their existence; if they did experience them, they destroyed their memory of it through forgetfulness. He argues that souls are not unbegotten, because newborn infants lack mind, reason, and understanding, and only gradually acquire them as the body grows. He concludes that the soul grows and develops together with the body, and that defects of the soul correspond to defects of bodily organs, just as the first-formed human body lay lifeless until God breathed into it.

outline.move: God fills all things and is not limited by place, and the divine is not subject to fixed laws and times; but since the philosophers clearly know they are caught in this difficulty, they change course and invent the myth of the water of forgetfulness.

Eustathius challenges the philosophers with a dilemma: if they escaped the drink of deception, then many others obviously did too; if they drank the water of forgetfulness like everyone else, how do they fabricate myths about souls? He adds that either way they are ignorant—if they didn't experience the waters, they don't know of their existence; if they did experience them, they destroyed their memory of it through forgetfulness—and traces their error to Egyptian superstition.
The age of newborn infants shows that souls are not unbegotten, because infants lack mind, reason, and understanding, and only gradually acquire them as the body grows.

The soul grows with the body and receives its powers gradually; those who remain foolish have defective souls corresponding to damaged bodily parts, and the first-formed body lay lifeless until God breathed into it.

voices.speaker: Eustathius (addressing Pythagoreans and Platonists)
voices.how_marked: Direct address with vocative plurals (ὦ Πυθαγόραι καὶ Πλάτωνες) and first-person plural verb (φαμεν) in the opening challenge; second-person plural verbs appear in u01-rem-early (ἐφύγετε, ἐγένεσθε, ἐπίετε, μυθοποιεῖτε, ἴστε)

key_terms.sense: The human soul, whose origin and nature are the subject of the treatise.
Unbegotten, not created, having no origin; the philosophical claim Eustathius denies.
Forgetfulness, especially the mythical water of forgetfulness that souls drink before birth.
The water of the mythical river of forgetfulness in philosophical accounts of the soul's descent.
Mind or intellect, a power of the soul that infants lack and gradually acquire.
Practical wisdom or prudence, a developed power of the soul.
Reason or rational speech, a power of the soul absent in infants.
The body, with which the soul grows and to whose organs the soul's powers correspond.
Newborn infant, whose lack of mental powers shows the soul is not unbegotten.
The first-formed human, Adam, whose body lay lifeless until God breathed into it.
The Creator or fashioner, God, who formed the first human body.
The image of God in which the first human was made.
Sleep, described as a condition common to body and soul.

scripture: The author cites the Psalms according to the Septuagint, referring to David's hymnody (τὴν τοῦ Δαυῒδ ὑμνολογίαν). Modern citations should use the Septuagint Psalm numbering, which generally matches the Hebrew numbering used in most English Bibles, with occasional differences; the specific Psalm is not identified in the fragment.
uncertain: The exact date of composition is unknown.
The specific Psalm of David being referenced is not identified in the fragment.
The original addressee or dedicatee of the treatise is not stated in the surviving fragments.
The full original structure of the treatise is unknown, since only fragments survive.

_unresolved_facts.claim: this appears to be directed against philosophical conceptions that would limit God
_unresolved_facts.fix: The opening statements about God filling all things and not being subject to laws and times are presented as positive theological affirmations, not as direct arguments against specific philosophical conceptions that limit God. The connection to limiting God is not explicitly made in the source.

_unresolved_facts.claim: if the philosophers escaped the drink of deception, then many others obviously did too, so the myth fails to explain universal ignorance
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Εἰ μὲν οὖν ὑμεῖς οἷοί· τε ἐγένεσθε τὸ τῆς πλάνης διαδρᾶναι πόμα, πρόδηλοι πολλοί τινες
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says 'if you were able to escape the drink of deception, then many are obviously [able to do so]'—the point is that many would be able to escape, not that many others obviously did escape. The argument is about the possibility of escape undermining the myth's explanatory power, not about actual universal ignorance.

_unresolved_facts.claim: if they did experience them, they destroyed their memory of it through forgetfulness
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: εἴτε τῆς πείρας αὐτῶν ἔσω γεγονότες, λήθῃ τὴν μνήμην τῆς χρήσεως αὐτῶν ἠφανίσατε καὶ τὴν γνῶσιν ἐξεπτύσατε
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text says they destroyed their memory of the use/experience (χρήσεως) of the waters through forgetfulness, and spat out the knowledge. The brief's 'destroyed their memory of it through forgetfulness' is tautological and imprecise; the Greek emphasizes they lost memory of the use/experience, not 'of it' vaguely.

_unresolved_facts.claim: God fills all things and is not limited by place, and the divine is not subject to fixed laws and times; but since the philosophers clearly know they are caught in this difficulty, they change course and invent the myth of the water of forgetfulness
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀλλ' ἐπειδὴ σαφῶς ἴσασιν ἁλισκομένους ἐντεῦθεν ἑαυτούς, μεταβαλλόμενοι πλάττουσιν τὸ τῆς λήθης ὕδωρ
_unresolved_facts.fix: The 'difficulty' (ἐντεῦθεν) refers to being caught/convicted by the preceding argument about God's omnipresence and freedom from temporal/spatial limits, not a general 'difficulty.' The philosophers know they are caught (ἁλισκομένους) by this argument specifically, and so change course and invent the myth.

_unresolved_facts.claim: He adds that either way they are ignorant—if they didn't experience the waters, they don't know of their existence; if they did experience them, they destroyed their memory of it through forgetfulness—and traces their error to Egyptian superstition
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Ἀλλ' εἰς ταῦτα βαρβαρώδη δεισιδαιμονίᾳ τραπέντες ἐσφάλησαν, Αἰγυπτίοις χρησάμενοι καθηγεμόσιν
_unresolved_facts.fix: The Egyptian superstition reference comes after the dilemma about ignorance, but the text says 'turning to these things through barbarian superstition, they erred, using Egyptians as guides'—the 'these things' (ταῦτα) refers to the myths/ideas discussed, and the dative δεισιδαιμονίᾳ is instrumental ('by superstition'), not 'to' superstition. The brief's 'traces their error to Egyptian superstition' slightly obscures that they used Egyptians as guides (καθηγεμόσιν) in turning to these ideas.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Followers of Pythagoras, addressed by Eustathius as representative philosophical opponents
_unresolved_facts.fix: The text addresses 'Πυθαγόραι' directly, but whether these are 'followers of Pythagoras' in a historical sense or Pythagoras himself addressed as a type is ambiguous. The plural could represent followers, but the direct vocative address treats them as present interlocutors.

_unresolved_facts.claim: first-person plural verb (φαμεν) in the opening challenge
_unresolved_facts.source_quote: Τί γάρ φαμεν, ὦ Πυθαγόραι καὶ Πλάτωνες
_unresolved_facts.fix: φαμεν is first-person plural, but it is not clearly 'in the opening challenge' as a marker of Eustathius's voice—it's part of the rhetorical question 'What do we say...?' which could be editorial plural or genuine plural address. The brief overstates its function as a voice marker.

_unresolved_facts.claim: Modern citations should use the Septuagint Psalm numbering, which generally matches the Hebrew numbering used in most English Bibles, with occasional differences
_unresolved_facts.fix: This editorial guidance about citation practice has no basis in the source text and is irrelevant to verifying the brief against the source. Remove or mark as editorial comment.
